utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please be seated. May we have the appearances, please, when we have heard, of course, the case number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, and Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Surprised to see you. But welcome back to The Hague, Mr. Lukic. Before we start with the link, you may know there is a problem, the German saying: "One shouldn't dance on two marriages at the same time." Unfortunately I have to do so. I won't call it a marriage, but on two procedures. So to be serious, the question is: Do we have the consent of the parties to continue with the videolink after I have to leave in about 10 minutes, under Rule 15 bis, the case then presided over by Judge Vassylenko, following our Rules of Procedure and Evidence? Are there any objections by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: By the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic in person?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. May we then ask the audio/video unit, the line to Banja Luka functions? I see it come up, and I can see Madam Dahuron. Very good afternoon to Banja Luka. First a sound check. Can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Banja Luka] [Indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's a little bit difficult in the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Banja Luka] Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, the quality is not the best. But if we continue this way, we have it in one minute. Can you continue speaking a little bit in English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Banja Luka] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's not that good.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Banja Luka] We are now trying to increase the quality. It's not very --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: During the time the connection should be improved. Could we have the usual view of the entire room.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Banja Luka] It's the same person doing both so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Banja Luka] Yes, I understood you. Do you understand when I talk?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, now it's better. May I ask Defence counsel present here in this courtroom, is there any request for protective measures of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't think so that there is any request for protective measures, but maybe Madam Registrar could confirm it with the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We'll try, as we did previously also.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, Madam Registrar, to escort the witness into your office in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Zvonko Iglic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May we please hear your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated, please. You should not be surprised that, say, within the next 10 minutes, Judge Vassylenko will preside over this case as to the fact that I have to return to another case. You are called as a Defence witness. May I ask, before starting with the examination-in-chief, Mr. Iglic, do you need any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't need any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. As you have been called by the Defence, the floor is now for the Defence. Mr. Lukic, please, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Iglic.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Branko Lukic, as you know, and together with Mr. John Ostojic, I represent Dr. Stakic before the Tribunal in The Hague. Would you please be so kind to introduce yourself for the record. Can you please tell us your first name and your last name.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: My name is Zvonimir Iglic. I live in Prijedor. I was born in 1949 in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us the name of your father.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Edgar is the name of my father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are you by profession, Mr. Iglic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: I'm a physician, and I have a residency -- I'm a specialist in otorhinolaryngology. I'm an ENT doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you graduate from the school of medicine?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the school of medicine in Novi Sad in 1974.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you complete your residence?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: I completed my residence in 1971, again, in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what is your ethnic background and what is your religion?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: I'm a Slovenian, and I suppose I should be Catholic. But my belief is somewhat different, so I cannot give you a decisive answer in terms of my religion, if that may mean anything to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether you were a member of any political party from the year 1980 onwards.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: In 1990, in the first multiparty elections, I was proposed as a deputy of the Municipal Assembly on behalf of the SDP which, in a way, continued the tradition of the League of Communists which ceased to exist in that year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the leader of the party that you belonged to at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: The leader of the party was professor of political sciences from Sarajevo, Mr. Turakovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you elected as a deputy to the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor in the first multiparty elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was elected as a deputy to the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us briefly, what would you say about the period following the multiparty elections up to the end of the period -- up to the end of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: After the multiparty elections, for the first time, the government, as I had expected, was distributed amongst the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ethnically-based parties. In Prijedor, the votes were largely divided between the SDS and the SDA. The SDP won a negligible number of seats in the Municipal Assembly, so it couldn't participate in the government, not even as a coalition partner. At that time, municipal organs were established, both the municipal organ and the executive organs, that is, and the sectors were distributed in the police, in the secretariats of the professional services in the municipality, and this was done as a joint effort and in cooperation with the people who were at that time in the leadership of the SDS and the SDA. Obviously, the SDP did not play any role in all that. It didn't have any influence. It was just a small opposition party that appeared for the first time in the multiparty municipal assembly. At that time, there was no need to form a coalition. There was no need to have an opposition because before that time, there was just one party. The relationships in the Municipal Assembly were, at the beginning, very correct. But different interests that existed among the two leading parties in the Prijedor Municipality resulted because of the distribution of the key sectors, resulted in a split between these two parties. At the beginning, it was believed that if something was postponed, then it would not blow into a major problem, and that it wouldn't be a problem in the distribution of power. In that way, without any problems, the offices of the president of the municipality, the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly, the president of the Executive Board were allocated, and the government started functioning. I must say that to my very big satisfaction, this happened, although I was a member of the party who -- which lost in the elections. But at that time, I did not have any political ambitions. I only believed that it was important that we have a multiparty system in the town because Prijedor was inhabited by various peoples and that it was very important that the votes of the people were evenly divided and they were given two different major ethnically-based parties. I don't know whether this has been enough for the moment, or do you want me to say something else that would pertain to that period?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it happen at the time that you would leave the sessions of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor because of the constant skirmishes between these two irreconcilable parties?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: As time went by, one could see things that I am still not clear on. We could see that very important sectors were left nonallocated. They were not allocated to any of the two ruling parties, either to the SDS or to the SDA. At those moments, the work of the Municipal Assembly was blocked, and this resulted in the physical exhaustion of the deputies. At least, I was physically exhausted by those long sessions of the Municipal Assembly that took place in the building of the national theatre in Prijedor. And that is why I left the last few sessions of the assembly, for a simple reason: I could no longer sit there because I was embittered. There was a bitter taste in my mouth, and I realised that such quarrels could not be without a bad result, a bad consequence for all of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Although this discord was reflected in the distribution of offices and positions, what actually was behind the discord between these two blocs? Was it the economic situation, the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or maybe something else?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: There were numerous reasons for which these two ethnic groups did not trust each other. It is obviously not possible to talk about all the causes of the conflict. It would simply take too much time. But I can say that I came to Prijedor without the legacy of the bad relationship between these two ethnic groups, and that's why I did not give it too much thought until the moment when these conflicts gave reason for concern to all of us. Obviously, there were economic reasons. The situation was getting worse in the former Yugoslavia, including Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was a high rate of unemployment. There was an -- increasingly less money, and people were becoming more and more warded [phoen]. And the problems obviously arose from the desire to salvage the so-called communism in the former Yugoslavia. When I say the "so-called communism," I didn't experience any other communism, so I don't know what other types of communism were in Eastern Europe or in the Soviet Union. But it was the desire of all of us to finally have a new kind of state, a multiparty political system. I didn't believe for a moment that the state would eventually break up, and especially not in the way it did. What has led to -- what has led to the conflict between these two people, I cannot say, but I witnessed this breakup, this conflict. This breakup had a bearing on all of us, regardless of our ethnic background. Serbs and Muslims formed a majority in Prijedor Municipality, and for that reason, the organisation of these two peoples, through their political leadership, first in Sarajevo and then elsewhere, led to these two ethnic groups becoming suspicious of each other. There was a fear amongst people because the leaderships of these two respective peoples started telling people that there was a threat, that people had to be mobilised, that they had to be ready. Those people who were in the position to listen to the news at the time could hear nothing else but those things. I did not at that time believe that there would be a fully-fledged conflict, but I did start suspecting that something like that might eventually happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor. Now I would like to ask you to explain to this Honourable Chamber, what was the situation like in Prijedor, and can you take Autotransport as an example? That is when the army requisitioned some of the buses, and this was approved by Mr. Nihad Suljanovic on behalf of Autotransport, and this gentleman was a Muslim. He was not the one who approved the requisitioning; he only signed this piece of paper. So can you tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: The then Yugoslav People's Army needed vehicles, and that's why they requisitioned some technical equipment, including the one part of the fleet of the Autotransport Prijedor transport company. The main dispatcher at the time was Nihad Suljanovic from Prijedor. He is an engineer, and he had the right and he was the one who was in the position to react to such a request of the army. He was the one who had the right to decide which vehicle to give to the army without impairing the transport services in the town of Prijedor. This is what he did. And the then-director obviously looked at that decision, and it was only normal that he complied with the request of the army. And Nihad Suljanovic was suspended from the job, and then he was fired. In that period, there was a war in Slavonia, and vehicles were requisitioned by the Yugoslav People's Army to serve the needs of the troops. We found this surprising, that there was a relationship which should have been absolutely defined. We knew that the requirements of the army should be a priority and that the attitude towards the army which requested the vehicles should have been different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the director of Autotransport who suspended Mr. Suljanovic, and what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: I don't know his name. I know that he held a Ph.D. in engineering, and I believe that he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we just clarify one thing. Can you please place this event in a year and a month. You mentioned Slavonia and troops leaving for Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: It was 1991. And as for the month, I am not sure what month was that. I believe that it was sometime in the autumn of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be enough about that event. Were you mobilised by the JNA, and from when until when did you serve in the army and in what way did you serve?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: In the then-Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, there was only one army, and that was the JNA. I received a general callup, and because, according to the then organisation of the medical corps, I belonged to one of the units of the JNA. I reported to the military department, to the command of this unit. I think it was the 318th Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Motorised Brigade. I may be wrong about the number, and I beg your pardon if I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it the 343rd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do apologise. Yes, it was the 343rd Brigade, that is, the Prijedor Brigade. My role in this brigade was thus completed because the brigade commander did not order me to put on a uniform or go anywhere in the field. I continued doing my job in the hospital, but as was the case with other colleagues, it was possible that I would be called upon when needed so that others who were active in the medical corps could go on leave and be replaced for a while. At that time, the institution of work obligation did not exist yet, so the callup by the unit was meant really that I was to be on standby. But it did not affect my work in the hospital in any way. I have to say that I was fortunate enough not to be called upon to go anywhere where there was fighting going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us, please, whether you remember until when this situation lasted and when you changed your status and how?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of January, 1993, the Ministry of Defence Prijedor department sent me a decision on work obligation, and with this, my military service ended as of the 5th of January, 1993. The work obligation referred to work in the hospital, and the decision contained my full name and profession. This work obligation was renewed from time to time because of possible changes in its content.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of 1992, 1993, and after that, what was your position in the Prijedor hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: From 1981, until two years ago, I held only one position, that of a specialist in otorhinolaryngology, and from 1991 to 1998, I was the head of this service. Throughout the period before the war, when we set up this service, five doctors passed through it, and just before the war there were five specialised doctors working there. In 1998, I continued working as a specialist in the same -- in the same ENT ward as a specialist. But when I became the head, I was replaced by my colleague Dr. Relja Mizkajic with whom I have to say I still have very correct relations, although we are not working any more. But we are still on friendly terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell us why you are no longer working with Mr. Relja?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: The overall situation in health care, especially in the Prijedor hospital in the last few years, has been deteriorating. It has been getting worse and worse in the financial aspect. And the problem was not just the very small salaries, the irregular salaries received by doctors at the moment seven months' late, but also the work conditions became worse and worse. And my ambition to continue this weakened. And then I decided to open up a private practice in accordance with the law passed and with the approval of the ministry of health, I have been working as the only person in my own practice. And to put it simply, I'm doing this in order that my family can survive. That's why I had to leave the hospital. So the only reason were the working conditions, the poor financial situation, the dissatisfaction among the employees. That was the only reason I left the hospital and opened up a private practice, in order to earn more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have been focussing on your work history, and this has led us up to the present time. I would now like to go back in time to the period when you were an assemblyman in the Prijedor Municipal Assembly. And I would like you to think about your office, the office that you held at that time. As an assemblyman in the Prijedor Municipal Assembly, do you know what was the relationship between the president of the Municipal Assembly and the Executive Board, and do you know what powers, if any, were held by the president of the Municipal Assembly in relation to organs such as the army, the police, and so on? Can you tell us from your own personal experience how you saw the office of the president of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, in the first days of the work of the assembly, apart from the fact that the deputies came from different parties, the work did not differ very much from what it had been before the multiparty elections. I mean, as far as the rules of procedure go. As far as I know, if I remember well, according to the statute of the municipality, both then and before that, the office of president and the deputy president of the municipality was a purely ceremonial one. He was not the highest authority of the municipality. I am speaking now of the period before the war. This was the place where decisions of the municipal committee and the League of Communists were implemented. And decisions were simply rubber-stamped by the municipality, by the Municipal Assembly. And when a multiparty assembly was set up, this still resembled the previous assembly. I think that the statutes and rules of procedure have to exist somewhere, but I believe that the office of president was not more important than established in the statute. And that neither before nor after the war did the president of the assembly have any special power or any special authority except, which is quite understandable, a certain amount of prestige, which is indubitable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When - speaking of Dr. Stakic's prestige in Prijedor - was he a well-known person in Prijedor, and can you describe his position in your town at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: It's quite clear that Dr. Stakic became well known when he became the president of the municipality. This was a public office, and when he became vice-president, he was seen on radio, on television, in the media. And of course, he thus became well known among the people in the town. But I have to go back to the period when these offices were allocated, as I mentioned, after the elections of 1990. At that time, Dr. Stakic, as a politician, I have to admit, was completely anonymous. He was not well known at all. I did know of him as a colleague, a fellow doctor. He was then a general practitioner. And because he worked in the same medical centre that I worked in, and the centre covered several municipalities of the then Bosnian Krajina, so I have to draw a distinction between him as a politician who most people in the town did not know at all and him as a doctor. But according to the hierarchy, if I remember well, he was the vice-president, which means that he had to help organise the work of the assembly and the sessions, and that's precisely what I remember. There were sessions, and there were discussions in the corridors, and this was in the period when there was still relative harmony or at least there were no open conflicts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the president of the Municipal Assembly was able to issue orders to the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly, or whether the Executive Board was responsible to the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: I will try to tell you what I know, although I was never involved in this kind of work, nor was I involved in politics before the war. But I'm sure that in the period before the multiparty elections, and I am deeply convinced that this situation continued after, that alongside the party structures of the then League of Communists and later on the parties ruling in Prijedor, the president of the Municipal Assembly had no real power. His was a purely ceremonial job. The duty of the president of the municipality was to go to public events, but I don't remember that the president of the municipality was ever someone who was able to run or manage the executive branch of government or the Executive Board and the municipal secretariats. This should be clear to everyone. I hope it is. And the secretariats were directly under the republican government after the events of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since we are now mentioning the secretariats, some of which later became republican ministries, did you ever see Mr. Cehajic while he was the president of the Municipal Assembly issuing orders to the Ministry of the Interior, that is, the police?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: I know of no such thing. No, I don't know. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Cehajic issuing orders to the army?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: No, I have no knowledge or information of this either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now talk about the period after the 30th of April, 1992, the period after the takeover of power. On the 1st day after the takeover of power, did you see Mr. Cehajic in Prijedor, and if you did, where and how did you see him?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: That morning came as a surprise to me because in spite of the conflicts that existed between the two leading parties in Prijedor, I expected that the situation would continue as it was, and then perhaps that they might even reach agreement about certain issues. On that morning, if I remember rightly, it was a sunny morning. I saw my former teacher, the then president of the municipality of Prijedor, Mr. Cehajic. I saw him sitting in front of a small cafe, or rather a barbecue shop owned by a man called Kapetanovic. As usual, he was nicely dressed, wearing a tie. I didn't talk to him. I just said "hello," as I always did, because he had been my teacher and because I remembered him with pleasure because he was a nice man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, I am referring to the period after April 1992, did you have any contacts with Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because of the nature of my job, I had contacts with him almost every day. And in view of the office he then held in the municipality, after this period, I saw him less often, and we had fewer contacts. But still, whenever I asked him for help in my work in the hospital, because Dr. Kovacevic was an anaesthesiologist and a very good one, he would come to the hospital and bypassing all the rules, he would turn up in the morning and assist as an anaesthesiologist and help me with surgery, especially with children when I had to remove tonsils. And before and after the war, I have to say that we worked very well as a team.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you continue working with Dr. Kovacevic in 1993, 1994, and after that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Kovacevic was the director of the hospital. And due to the nature of our job, we continued working together in the operation theatre. And he was the director of the hospital in very difficult times for the health care, and he was the only person who could help me in my daily work. He was the only person responsible for all the problems that may have arisen, and he asked me to consult with him about any problems that I may have experienced with the personnel, with the resources. So we had daily contacts. But let me add to that, that our contacts were only in the hospital, and although they were in the hospital, sometime they were very informal because that's the kind of person Dr. Kovacevic was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the contacts with Dr. Kovacevic, did you ever feel that you were being treated differently because you were not a Serb? Did you feel awkward in those contacts?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: My relationship with Dr. Kovacevic was the relationship of two professionals, and it was also a friendly relationship. He was a bit older than me, and he had lived in the conditions much worse than my conditions were. But he was always ready to help; he was very professional; he could always give me very professional advice. He was a very good anaesthesiologist as I've already said. He worked as an anaesthesiologist for other services, but I always felt that he had time for me, that he always had the time to listen to me. Sometimes in the morning, we would meet, and we would talk very informally. Sometimes, we would even light a cigarette. He would sometimes come into the operating theatre with a cigarette in his mouth and I would scold him for that without any problems. That means that I had a lot of credit with him. He was not a quick tempered person as people thought he was. Those people who knew him better knew that he was a good person and that he couldn't hate anybody, on the contrary. This is what I know of him and this is what I thought of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to Dr. Kovacevic, did you also have contacts with another colleague of yours, Dr. Milomir Stakic in that period that we have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: In the period when Dr. Stakic was the president of the Municipal Assembly, my contacts with him were only formal. That means that we would only talk about certain things that pertained to the area of health care. I believe that it isn't difficult to understand that somebody who is a doctor and who finds himself in the role of the president of the Municipal Assembly is in the position to help the hospital in terms of heating, in terms of supplies. Sometimes it was so cold, there was no heating, we could skate on the floors of the hospital. So our contacts were mostly at the time when he came to visit the hospital. I always mustered the courage, despite his high position, to talk to him and to ask him for supplies from the humanitarian aid. And sometimes we even managed to obtain some things in that way -- in that way. So when I talked to Dr. Stakic, it was not to talk to the president of the Municipal Assembly, but to talk to a fellow doctor who could help me in my everyday work with my patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your contacts with Dr. Stakic, did you ever notice that you were being treated differently or worse than other people because you were not a Serb? And can you also tell us whether you ever concluded from Dr. Stakic's statements or behaviour that he hated Muslims and Croats and other non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: In my every contact with him, there was a very normal level of human respect, mutual respect. His handshake was very firm, and he always asked me whether there were any problems, whether we could manage. He was always very serious. I could never make him smile, let alone laugh. But he knew what our conditions of work were like, and that's why every conversation with him started with the words "Are you okay?" "Can you manage?" "Are there any problems?" He knew that we were short of supplies, and whenever we received supplies, we received very little. He, as I say, is a doctor, and he wanted to know about the work in the hospital. He didn't need to talk to me about politics. And I never felt in his relationship towards me any animosity or discrimination. I'm a Slovenian. I'm not using your term non-Serb, which I resent a little, because it puts all the Serbs on one side and the other people on the other side. And this cannot be the case. This is discriminatory. If you want to use it, okay, maybe you want to use it to explain some things that were happening at that time. In any case, I have to say that my contacts with him were always very correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I have to apologise. It was not my intention to insult anybody. We are just using the terms from the indictment, and that is why I'm using this term which I must admit I also find very strange.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: I believe that we think the same, although we are using these very formal terms. I did not mean to correct you. I know that you're using the terms that are customary in the indictment, and that have been used before. And I believe that we understand each other, that we are not talking at crosspurposes here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We absolutely understand each other. Thank you very much. In addition to the shortage of medicines in the Prijedor hospital, was there also a shortage of electricity, and were there any other shortages?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: The overall situation at the hospital in the beginning of the war was relatively good. The stocks of the medical corps of the Yugoslav People's Army and the stock of the medical stock of the hospital at the beginning met the needs. As we're talking about the medical supplies which are for -- which are used only once, and you never know how much will be used. These stocks begin to dwindle. And when I say medical supplies, I'm not talking only about gauzes and dressings and other things, but everything that is used in the everyday work of doctors, the syringes, catheters, all the things that are used only once and are then discarded when used. New medical supplies did not arrive, and there was no Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. electricity. We shared the lot of the entire town. We had a generator, a powerful generator, but that generator used oil, so we actually couldn't use it. Since we couldn't use that large generator, we had to use some small ones. I personally had a 300-watt generator that worked as a small aircraft engine. I used that when I went to the surgery, and I would take that generator and I would safeguard it as the apple of my eye. That generator used petrol, and petrol at that time was also a very precious commodity. All in all, I kept that little generator under a lock in my room. It was so precious to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Talking about the hospital, we know that Dr. Stakic came back to the hospital in 1993 and that he worked as Dr. Kovacevic's deputy. At that time, as a doctor, what was Dr. Stakic's reputation and what was the attitude of other colleagues towards Dr. Stakic at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: At that time, if my memory serves me well, there was the health centre as a medical institution. There was also a hospital and the medical centre, and I believe at that time, Dr. Stakic was the deputy of the director of the health centre, if I'm not mistaken. I don't want to get mixed up on his position. He was not the deputy director of the hospital, if my memory serves me right. And as far as the second part of your question is concerned, let me answer that: The colleagues who worked with him in Omarska knew him well. Most of the others didn't know him, which is understandable. When a young doctor starts working, it takes him at least ten years to gain a name, to become recognisable through his work, through his practice, depending on the specialisation. At that time, Dr. Stakic was a general practitioner. As far as I'm concerned, I -- my attitude towards him was neither positive or negative. I did not have any special opinion on his medical skills and knowledge. The majority of my colleagues did not know him. I'm talking about the colleagues who worked at the hospital. And as far as his political position is concerned, I'm not familiar with that, and I don't want to claim something that wouldn't be true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when Dr. Stakic came back to the medical centre of Prijedor, did Dr. Kovacevic ever tell you to treat people differently depending on their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dr. Stakic ever tell you to treat people differently depending on their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was a shortage of medicines; there was a lack of electricity, medical supplies, as you've said. Was there also a shortage of personnel in the provision of health care in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately there was. There was an increased number of wounded. The standard of living went down. The number of sick people went up. And this put our medical institution in a difficult situation, and the people who had remained working in the hospital after all the incidents had a tough job. Those colleagues who were surgeons such as gynecologists and ophthalmologists were not prepared, were ill-equipped, to take over the treatment of fresh wounds. We must bear in mind that throughout the war in Prijedor, from the front lines, in Krupa, Novi Grad, and especially Suva Medja [phoen], we received a huge number of wounded. Sometimes they were transported by helicopters, sometimes by ambulances. And that the first doctors who saw them were the ones in Prijedor. And this all meant that all of us doctors had to work around the clock. We barely had time to go home, have a bite to eat, and a shower. At that time, in the hospital, we did not have facilities for that. So there were people who left, but not because of that. Maybe we were tired, we were exhausted at that time, but we didn't complain. I don't remember that anybody complained. We all pulled our strings together and worked hard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Despite all of these problems and troubles, did it ever happen that groups of drunken people, armed people, barged into the hospital? Can you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: The Prijedor hospital is very big. There was a control of -- at one entrance, there was a group of policemen from the reserve force, mostly young men from Cirkin Polje. That is where the hospital is situated. So these young men were providing formal protection for the employees and for the patients, because it did happen sometimes unfortunately that lads who had gotten drunk in a cafe or in a pub decided to barge into the hospital on their way home. And that's when problems started. They would insult doctors and other personnel regardless of who they were. And the police role as protectors was rather weak. They couldn't protect us. However, there were no major incidents. There were some individuals who caused trouble, but I believe that they are known, and they have been punished for that. But in any case, there were no major incidents, just the incidents when drunken lads would barge into the surgery to see who was being treated, who was not being treated, whether there were wounded brought in and so on and so forth. All this disturbed the work of the medical personnel and decreased our level of service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of 1992, did you leave Bosnia and Herzegovina? Did you go anywhere outside the country, and did you get certain passes to do this, and who did you get them from?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1992 and 1993, I didn't leave the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. My need to go temporarily to Novi Sad occurred in 1994 when my eldest was to enroll at university in Novi Sad, and we needed a pass to do this. As a person subject to work obligation, and the same applied to persons who had been mobilised and were serving in the army, they had to have a pass issued by the Ministry of the Interior with the permission of high-ranking officers of the army of Republika Srpska. That is, the 1st Banja Luka Corps. I tried to pass through without such a permit, but I failed. I wasn't trying to run away. I had left my family in Prijedor. But then I tried to obtain such a pass for myself and for my son, who was already of age and he had just graduated from secondary school. And so I turned to Dr. Stakic who was a colleague of mine and who said to me very kindly but very firmly that he was unable to issue a pass of this kind and that he did not know how it could be obtained bypassing the police. Following his advice, I went to see the chief of police in Prijedor, the late Simo Drljaca, and I have to say that with his assistance and the assistance of people from the Ministry of the Interior in Bijeljina, I received a pass signed by the proper authorities, and then I was able to travel without any problems. And I have to say that I didn't have the feeling that Stakic didn't want to help me; I knew that he couldn't. It was simply not within his sphere of competence at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Iglic, I think we will now suggest that we take a break. We shall see whether it is a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: How much time you need to complete your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we need another quarter of an hour or 20 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: We have to have a break at 1600 hours, so you can complete your examination until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have heard, so we shall continue and complete the examination-in-chief. Dr. Iglic, did you know a person by the last name of Zeljaja, and do you know where this man comes from?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: The person named Zeljaja was a high-ranking army officer, but I couldn't tell you exactly what he was by the establishment. But he came to replace the then commander of the Prijedor military unit who was then a Lieutenant-Colonel, and his name was Arsic. I later learned that Zeljaja came from Sarajevo, or the surroundings of Sarajevo, because his father moved to Prijedor and came to me for checkups. That's how I know that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Zeljaja came from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where Mr. Arsic came from? You mentioned him.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Arsic, who was a captain first-class when the war broke out was an officer of the JNA. I know that he comes from Serbia. I think he was born in a village near Kopaonik, either Blace or Prokuplje, but I can't be sure. I don't have any precise knowledge as to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So neither Mr. Zeljaja nor Mr. Arsic were from the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether they knew Dr. Stakic before the war, either of these two gentlemen?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge of this. I know that by virtue of his post, the then commander of the Prijedor Brigade once addressed the Municipal Assembly, and I assume that he must have then been formally introduced to Dr. Stakic. I think that Dr. Stakic must have been introduced to him then. I think that he was already a major or perhaps even a lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned his speech in the Municipal Assembly. Can you tell us what reactions this speech prompted.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Arsic, by the establishment, was an officer of the unit when the unit was part of the JNA. And that's how he happened to be in Prijedor when the war broke out. His attitude towards us, assemblymen, at that time was very correct, and I am referring to all the assemblymen in the theatre. We had to use the theatre because it was large enough to hold the large number of assemblymen. This was the beginning of political pluralism, and he spoke in very specific terms. He told all of us that if there was no agreement between the political players in the town at the time, we would be contributing to the spreading of conflicts. And I assume he was then a major - he's a general now, Arsic. He was very convincing, and he spoke very decisively. Like every officer, he was wearing a uniform. And although his speech was very correct, it caused a lot of dissatisfaction on the other side of the theatre, that is, the then assembly. And I'm referring to the Benches where the representatives of the Muslim party usually sat. At that moment, I had a gut feeling, and I later on analysed the behaviour of these people in uniform, and I have to say that I was really not frightened by this speech. But people obviously had reasons to be afraid. Because at that time, members of the same army commanded by Arsic, these people were of all ethnicities, Muslims, Croats, Serbs. This was our unit. It was not a Serb unit or a Croat unit or a Muslim unit. And that's why I thought there was no reason to be afraid at that time. And I have to say that that's why I responded to the callup, because at that time, the unit was our unit. It was our common unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that point, it was probably 1991, am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the impression that the civil authorities, such as the Municipal Assembly to which you yourself belonged and the Executive Board, were able to issue orders to Mr. Arsic as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Neither then nor later, especially not later, did I have the feeling that any of the representatives of the civilian government in Prijedor, and by this, I mean the people holding offices in the municipality, were able to issue orders of any kind to the police, especially not to the chief of police, or any of the officers commanding the military units. The military hierarchy had been taken over from the JNA. And anybody who knows anything about this must know that before the war, the JNA was, I must say, a state within a state, so to speak. Perhaps someone wanted to give the impression that they had so much power that they could influence the decisions of the army or the police at that time. But it was certainly not the then president or the people around him who could do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "president," do you mean the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any situations in which it was evident that there were problems in communication between the municipal organs and the police, although they both belonged to the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: The relationship between the police and the civil government, well, it probably existed. It must have. But I don't know anything about the details, except that in the hospital, because we needed to obtain fuel, there were often conflicts between the director of the hospital and the representative of the military authorities concerning the transport of the wounded to Banja Luka because there was not enough fuel. And I have to say that Dr. Kovacevic, as he has been described by people, and so he was, he was quiet rough and prone to anger, because he couldn't understand that an army that was capable of waging war was unable to obtain fuel for the transport of the wounded. And this was within our sphere of confidence -- competence because the hospital was part of the military medical corps, although it was treating the wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have two more questions connected with Dr. Stakic's personality. Although you have already given a partial answer to this question, but I will ask you for some additional clarification, did Dr. Stakic ever in your presence advocate nationalist theories? Was he ever an advocate of nationalist policies?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: All my contacts with Dr. Stakic had to do with practical reasons. By, this I want to say that we were never friends who visited each other, chatted, or spent their leisure time together. But we did have opportunities - I think everybody is aware that in that period, the cafe or the restaurant called Oskar near the hospital was a place where we would always drop in to have a cup of coffee on our way to work. And very often, there was a group of colleagues there going to work or leaving work. And so it happened that I would find myself sometimes sitting in company with Dr. Stakic, not just the two of us, but we would be part of a group where it was possible to express one's opinions, one's feelings. And I never heard any hostile words expressed by him against non-Serbs. Never heard him say that. And I can state that decisively. I never heard him say anything bad about anyone, either an individual or an ethnic group. I never heard Dr. Stakic say anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you to tell us what your view was and is now of the reputation, character, and integrity of Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Before I decided to testify in Dr. Stakic's case before this Tribunal, I didn't analyse anyone's personality, with the exception, perhaps, of Dr. Kovacevic. But I have to say that I did make an analysis of Dr. Stakic's personality, and I will now state it in public hoping I will not offend anyone. I know that at that time, a young man being offered a political career would have found it difficult to refuse an office because as a doctor, he would have to be humane. And this should be more important to him than anything else. He did not refuse this offer. Had times been different, I don't believe he would have taken up a career in politics. But however hard he may have wanted to, he was unable to leave his stamp on events because when I tried to make my own analysis of the situation, most of the people who entered politics at the time didn't really have any personal gain. I never saw him storming or raging on about political issues, and I don't see that short of running away, how he could have done anything to prevent what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Iglic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This completes the examination-in-chief. After the break, you'll be examined by my learned friends from the Prosecution, and then by their honours, the Judges. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. May I ask Madam Registrar to be in touch with Banja Luka in order to restart our hearing at 16.35. Trial stays adjourned until 16.35. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Just for the transcript, the Trial Chamber continues in its entire composition. Based on a perusal of the LiveNote that happened beforehand, I take it that it's now for the Prosecution to cross-examine the witness. Correct? The examination-in-chief has been concluded. So may we see whether the link to Banja Luka is established. Okay. I don't know why, but on some screens, you can see the witness, and on others not. Now it's okay. Thank you. May I ask now the Prosecution to cross-examine the witness. Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Ms. Sutherland:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Iglic, I'm going to be asking you questions on behalf of the Prosecution. If you don't hear my question, please say so, and I will repeat it. Or if you don't understand it, I will try and rephrase it. During the questioning, I will also be making some references to pages numbers for the Court. And you don't have to be concerned with that. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're married to a woman of Serb ethnicity. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to Dr. Stakic about attaining a pass in 1994 - and this is on page 23, for the Defence and Your Honours - this was when Stakic was no longer the president, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: If my memory serves me right, then you are right. He was no longer president.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were giving evidence earlier on, you said that you asked Dr. Stakic for supplies for humanitarian aid for the hospital. And this is at page 17. This was because Stakic was the president of the Municipal Assembly and president of the Crisis Staff, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the president of the Municipal Assembly is the most prestigeous position in the municipality. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: According to the statute of the Municipal Assembly, I must say once again, I'm sure you can obtain a copy of that statute. The office of the president of the Municipal Assembly is ceremonial. When I say that, I'm not undermining the office of the president of the Municipal Assembly, but his authorities are somewhat limited in comparison with the authority of the executive power. And when I turned to him for help, it is only understandable. He was a doctor, and he was the president of the Municipal Assembly. Humanitarian organisations were in constant contact with the highest official of the municipality, and there was the officials of the municipality had an insight into what can be obtained from the humanitarian aid that arrived from Germany, from Greece. They knew what could be obtained. I personally got some supplies from Switzerland, and it was Dr. Stakic who helped me in the following way: I submitted to his office our requirements for certain instruments, and we obtained them from Switzerland. We call them Swiss instruments, although the proper name of those instruments is something totally different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Iglic, I want you to answer only the question that I put to you, and I will repeat my question for you. That is, the president of the Municipal Assembly is the most prestigeous position in the municipality, is it not? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: During the war, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your view, what position was higher than the president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: The chief of the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the president of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: I didn't know of the existence of the Crisis Staff for a long time. It was only when I had problems with fuel, then I was told that I should go to the Crisis Staff of my local commune to get the certificate for the purchase of fuel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Iglic, did you attend any Municipal Assembly sessions after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever invited to any meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a deputy. Why weren't you invited to any meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: I was a deputy representing the SDP, and that party, before the takeover and after the takeover was an opposition party. And it was the SDS that took over the entire power into its hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cedomir Vila represented the SDP party, did he not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was a Serb, of Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned oil again a moment ago. You said that there was no oil for the hospital in your evidence in chief, and this was at page 18. Do you know who made the decision that oil would go to the police and the Omarska camp, but not the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: No, madam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also testified at page 21 that there was an increase in the wounded, but a decrease in the number of persons to provide health care. This was at the same time as Croat and Muslim doctors were being dismissed and arrested and taken to the camps, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said earlier that there were no major incidents that occurred at the hospital in relation to unauthorised people entering the hospital. And this was at page 22. Do you know of an incident involving Zoran Zigic, a taxi driver, where he entered the hospital and shot a non-Serb in the chest -- I'm sorry, he didn't shoot him; he stabbed him.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was never arrested or prosecuted for this, was he, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This question is not based on the facts, and it's not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You want to respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is based on facts, and it was put to the witness and he agreed with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He said "I don't have that information." And I think that you have the information that Mr. Zigic was prosecuted for this criminal act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think we need not go into further dispute because the witness clearly stated, "I don't have that information." So may I ask --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was -- I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Iglic, you stated a moment ago, and this is at page 29, that Dr. Stakic didn't refuse the political office and had times been different, he wouldn't have taken up a career in politics. Are you aware that Dr. Stakic entered politics of his own volition, that he founded Omarska branch of the People's Radical Party Nikola Pasic? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that Dr. Stakic was the first president of the People's Radical Party Nikola Pasic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What was the question? Is this a new question or did you just rephrase the previous one?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did. And it was very disjointed. Are you aware that Dr. Stakic was the first president of the People's Radical Party Nikola Pasic in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that he was a deputy for the Municipal Assembly on the SDS list?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: That, I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that he was appointed vice-president --

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that he was a member of the SDS. No. I'm sorry, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not aware that he was appointed vice-president of the SDS in September 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that he took over the position of president of the Municipal Assembly after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That Dr. Stakic was president of the Crisis Staff, the Prijedor Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that Dr. Stakic became president of the municipality again after the war?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you please repeat the question. I have problems with this connection, with the line. So I have missed parts of your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. My last question was this: Do you know that Dr. Stakic became president of the Prijedor Municipality again after the war?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: No, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If all these things were true that I've just put to you about Dr. Stakic's political career, would they change your opinion about his political ambitions?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: I believe that there's no physician should enter into politics, and I believe the same of Dr. Stakic. I believe that his involvement in politics was a mistake. He should have stuck to medicine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, Dr. Iglic, were any of your friends or colleagues mistreated, arrested, or detained in any of the camps in the Prijedor Municipality between May and September 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name them for the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: My colleague Dr. Esad Sadikovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened -- what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: After the war, I have learned that he was no longer among the living.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name any other of your friends or colleagues that were mistreated or detained.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Among my colleagues, I don't know of anybody. But I heard there was Dr. Osman Mahmuljin, and a Dr. Nevad Basic was in Trnopolje. He was the youngest of my fellow ENT doctors from the department of otorhinolaryngology in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any crimes that these people committed which would have resulted in their detention in one of these camps?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier, Dr. Iglic, that you knew Muhamed Cehajic. In the meetings that you had with Dr. Stakic, did you ever ask him about Muhamed Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I can have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Iglic, in any of the conversations that you had with Dr. Stakic, did he ever ask about what happened to these doctors that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have only one question. You mentioned on page 36, line 5, that Dr. Esad Sadikovic was no longer among the living, as you told us. Later, you stated that you are not aware that Dr. Esad Sadikovic ever was a suspect of having committed a crime. So the question before us is always the same: Why was it that Dr. Esad Sadikovic disappeared and is no longer among the living? I think, as a colleague of yours, you have given some thoughts to this question.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes. If I may, I will explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Dr. Sadikovic was a colleague of mine, and also a friend of mine. We visited either other. He was my friend. He was a joker, and he was a very professional, skillful doctor. I don't even want to think about his possible crimes. And as of his disappearance and of his tragic lot, I can only say that this has had a huge impact on me, and I still feel the sadness for the fact that he is not amongst us, that I don't have the opportunity to be friends with him any longer. I simply was not in the position to help him in any way. I was not in a position to find out where he was at the moment when he disappeared nor what happened to him. All the information that I have about his lot I had after the war. Dr. Sadikovic disappeared. I don't know when. I can only assume that it was at the beginning of the war. But to this very day, it will happen to me that I see somebody who looks like him, and I will hope that it will be him because we were not just colleagues; we were really good friends. So I always mistake other people for him, wishing that it was him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever have an opportunity, maybe later, even after the war or maybe in 1992, to discuss the fate of your common colleague, Dr. Esad Sadikovic, with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have such an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I may pass the floor to Judge Vassylenko, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Dr. Iglic, you described the position of the president of the Municipal Assembly as ceremonial one. Then why you discussed the practical problems related to the health care with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: By coincidence, the president of the municipality was a physician. I've tried to explain why we went to see him. We relied on humanitarian sources for supplies, for the hospital. And it is only logical that in such a position we, so to say, abused Dr. Stakic's position. The humanitarian aid at that time arrived in Prijedor after contacts with the president of the municipality, the president of the Red Cross. And they were at the source of the information on the humanitarian aid. The reasons are simple. Anybody who came from abroad to bring humanitarian aid would be received by the president of the municipality. That is why I contacted the president of the municipality, knowing that anybody who had arrived with the humanitarian aid would have contacted the president of the municipality first, or any other officials of the municipality. They were the ones who could tell me if anything had arrived or what had arrived. And that is why I, so to say, abused Dr. Stakic, who was my fellow physician and who happened to be the president of the municipality. I don't know what other explanation I can offer to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Why didn't you address to Dr. Kovacevic, who was the president of the Executive Board of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kovacevic worked with me, and he was the end user of the same medical supplies from the humanitarian aid. I told you already that at the beginning, we had enough medicines and supplies because we had stocks from the JNA. Later on, from different parts of the world, from Greece, Germany, Switzerland, the nations arrived. We had a huge supply of medical necessities from France. This was partly used and partly it was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. incompatible with all the equipment that we had at the time. So it is then logical. Dr. Kovacevic was the end user of the same supplies that I used. We both used the same things. And it was not up to Dr. Kovacevic to obtain any of those supplies. And I'm sorry to say, but Dr. Kovacevic at the time when he was the president of the Executive Board also worked as an anaesthesiologist in the hospital. I believe that I've already said that in my testimony. I've already -- I also told you that I would sometimes ask him to assist me with an operation, which he would do first thing in the morning. And he would help me as an anaesthesiologist on my team when I performed operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Dr. Iglic, are you aware that in the 1980s, at the beginning of the 1990s, the position of the president of Municipal Assembly ex officio was the position of the president of people's Defence council?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: No. At that time I was in no way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Argibay, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Iglic, good afternoon. I have a couple of questions for you. You told us earlier that you were surprised on the morning of April the 30th about the takeover by the SDS in Prijedor. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Weren't you aware that the SDS had already formed a Serbian Municipal Assembly in January 1992 in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Weren't you aware that the deputies -- the municipal deputies from the SDS had abandoned the Municipal Assembly in Prijedor before that time?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: No. If my memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: But you were a deputy at that moment. Do you remember which assembly session was the last one you attended?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: I believe it was the session during which there was a discord and disagreement about the appointment of a candidate to an office in the police. And this is the session that I left because it lasted way too long, and it was difficult for me to sit there for hours on end and listen to the parties arguing forever. I listened to the session in my car on the radio in my car. My car was parked in the parking lot behind the national theatre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And what was the outcome of the long session?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: I believe that the outcome was actually the interruption of the session, and that after that, the assembly never met again in its full composition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Nor approximately the month or something? Was it the end of 1991, beginning or 1992 more or less?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: It may have been the autumn of 1991. I don't think it was winter or early spring. However, I reserve the right to say that I'm not sure about the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any questions in return by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only two, Your Honour. Further examination by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Iglic, that's me again. You have mentioned, or somebody has mentioned the name of Mr. Nikola Pasic, which gave the name to Dr. Stakic's party. Are you aware that Dr. Nikola Pasic was the first prime minister of the first Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My second question has to do with one of your remarks. When you compared the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor with the theatre, and at the same time sessions of the assembly were held in the theatre --

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the representatives of the Muslim people were sitting on one side of the theatre.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that these benches were occupied by the Muslims who belonged to other parties, not only to the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Yes. The then president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor belonged to the party of entrepreneurs, and he was also sitting on that side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us his name, although I believe that we all know his name.

utterances.speaker: ZVONIMIR IGLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Murselovic, a friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I also thank the Honourable Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any questions by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is not the case. Then I have to thank you, Dr. Iglic, for coming to the office and to testify in this case, assisting us in coming closer to the truth. Thank you very much. And this concludes today's videolink. And may I just Madam Dahuron, can we continue as scheduled with the witness tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Banja Luka] Yes, Your Honour, Witness number 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, once again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Banja Luka] Yes, Your Honour. We will proceed tomorrow with Witness Number 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. And final question to Madam Dahuron, what about the additional and final 92 bis statement? Is it on its way?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Banja Luka] I will let you know as soon as possible. It was rescheduled [Indiscernible] as soon as possible, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I take it that it will happen, the one to be taken in Banja Luka, during this week. Thank you very much also for all the assistance in Banja Luka for providing us this videoconference in this excellent quality. Thank you, this concludes the videolink. I take it that Witness 077 is available. I think it would be appropriate to have a short break now, and then to continue. Any protective measures requested?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the trial stays adjourned until 5.35. --- Break taken at 5.16 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Rosic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. Good day. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we hear your solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You are called as a witness for the Defence. May I, therefore, give the floor to the Defence. Mr. Ostojic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Ostojic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, good afternoon. My name is John Ostojic --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I wish to greet this Court, this international Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. As I stated, my name is John Ostojic, and along with Branko Lukic, we represent Dr. Milomir Stakic.
