I'm going to ask you a series of questions here today, so please be patient, and if there's a question that you do not understand fully, ask -- or tell me so and I will attempt to clarify that question for you so that you will fully understand the question and give us your most truthful and honest answer. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, can you please state your full name, first and last name, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: My name is Branko Rosic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May we have your date of birth, sir.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: The 31st of January, 1936.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you were born and in which municipality.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: In the village of Busnovi, municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, forgive me for asking this question. What is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: By ethnic background, I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, where did you reside in the spring and summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I lived in my area, and I was employed in the iron ore mine of Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The area in which you lived, in your area, is that also located in the municipality known as the Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Share with us, if you will, sir, your educational background. Did you attend any school, and if so, can you please tell us which school and when you graduated.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: I went to primary school, and I attended secondary school. So I have completed secondary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And share with us, if you will, sir, briefly your employment history and background. Where were you employed immediately after completion of your educational studies?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: It's a long time since I completed my schooling. I'm old now. After my schooling, I started work, and I held several jobs. But at that time, I was working in the Omarska iron ore mine. I was a pump operator, operating the pumps and maintaining the pumps for water at deep levels and surface water and drinking water and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get to your employment at the iron ore mine in just a few minutes. I'm just trying to obtain some quick background information so that we can have a better appreciation of who you are. And thank you for that. Sir, with respect to any political affiliations, in 1990, were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us which party you were a member and state for us whether you were an active or passive member of that particular party.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Well, I was a passive member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, sir, attend regularly the meetings of the SDS from 1990 throughout any significant period of time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us the time parametres in which you were employed at the iron ore mine at Omarska, from what period of time to approximately what period of time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: You mean the years, or how do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: From 1983, I worked in the Omarska mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, did you work in the Omarska iron ore mine in the spring and summer of 1992 as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just briefly share with us what your job duties and obligations were while you were employed at the iron ore mine at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: I maintained the water system. I was the pump operator in the mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to take you to a period of approximately ten years ago, the spring and summer of 1992. And I would respectfully ask that you concentrate on that period of time for the purposes of my next following questions. With respect to the iron ore mine, sir, did you continue to be employed there under your regular employment duties or was there a work obligation that was issued to you to work at the iron ore mine as a pumper, as you state, maintaining the water system in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the question, because due to the fact that you put several questions together, the "yes" is not quite clear to which part.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I think it's probably the first time I've done that, so my apologies to the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let me ask the question if I may once again. Did you in the summer of 1992 receive a work obligation to continue to work at the Omarska iron ore mine?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had a work obligation, and I worked throughout this period in the mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the period specifically we're interested or that I'm interested in is the period of time that there were detainees at the iron ore mine in the summer of 1992. Is that when, sir, you were under a work obligation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to be a little more specific with my questions now. Sir, we've established essentially that approximately the end of April, April 30th, 1992, there was a takeover in the Prijedor Municipality. Did you continue to work in the iron ore mine after April 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I continued working there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, sir, do you know when detainees were brought to the iron ore mine in the summer or spring of 1992? And if you don't know the exact date, I believe we can understand that. Can you give us the approximate date in which you recall that detainees were brought to the iron ore mine?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: They were brought there approximately towards the end of May, around that time. But I can't tell you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's for my next several questions just use those milestones that you have set for us, the end of April, April 30th, 1992, up until the time that the first detainees were brought to the iron ore mine, as you stated "towards the end of May 1992." During that period of time, sir, did you continue to work in the same fashion that you had prior to April 30th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I continued to work. I had a work obligation, and I continued working as usual. I continued doing the same job that I had done before that. I operated the pumps, maintained the water system, and I just stayed there and worked as I had before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that three- or four-week period that we've established here, was there any changes in the iron ore mine at all before the detainees came? Was there any plan or organisational structures that were changed during that three- to four-week period?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: There were some changes. There were some changes. People didn't show up for work, people of other ethnic groups. They failed to turn up for work for a time. I don't know why. But that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's discuss if we will changes in the physical structure of the iron ore mine during that three- to four-week period, were there any actual changes to the physical structure of the iron ore mine, such an erection of a fence, such as removal of certain material outside or inside to make accommodations for any particular rooms? Were any types of those things done within that three- to four-week period at the iron ore mine?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: No, nothing happened. No changes took place. Everything remained normal. Everything was the same as before except that people didn't come to work regularly. So I don't know what happened because of that. But something started. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Staying with this time period, if we may, did there come a time within that three- to four-week period -- let me strike that and start from the beginning. During this three- to four-week period, did the military or the police begin to make any preparations in the iron ore mine at Omarska where you worked and where you continued to be gainfully employed on a regular and continuous basis?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: No preparations were carried out according to me. We worked in shifts. And during my shift, I didn't notice any preparations. But I had a 24-hour shift, and then I would be off for 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, with respect to the period that the detainees were being brought to the Omarska iron ore mine, were you, sir, present when the detainees were initially brought to the iron ore mine in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was present when they were brought in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you stated, I believe, that that was sometime at the end of May 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, about then, the end of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, who brought the detainees to the iron ore mine.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: The detainees were brought by the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that day, when you first saw the detainees being brought to the iron ore mine by the military -- or army it's quoted as saying, did anyone notify you, sir, in advance that detainees would be brought to the iron ore mine?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody said anything about me. I knew nothing about it. I only saw them when they arrived in buses. People were objecting, protesting. People didn't want them to be brought to the mine. But the military did what they wanted. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, that day when the detainees were brought, sir, how many and in what mode -- strike that. Let me break down the question so I don't ask a compound question here. Sir, that day when you saw the initial detainees come into the Omarska iron ore mine, how did they arrive? I know you said the bus -- a bus. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, in buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many buses on that initial day came with detainees to be placed in the iron ore mine?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: There was more than one bus. About 20, but I didn't count them, so I couldn't tell you the number. There were many buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time, sir, did you notice what the military force was in terms of the number of personnel that they had? How many military men were transporting these detainees to the iron ore mine?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: There were many of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, or at any subsequent time, sir, were you asked or instructed and ordered to wear a certain type of insignia or designation in order for the military to know you and differentiate you from the detainees?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes. We wore white armbands on one arm. We had white armbands so that we could be recognised. There were a lot of military around. And this enabled me to go to my workplace. I had to have this armband, and then I was able to go to my place of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just in order to set another time line or milestone, can you tell us from the end of May when the detainees first arrived, to the best of your recollection, when did the detainees -- when were they moved out of the iron ore mine in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: They started taking them away maybe -- well, they were there for maybe two months or a month and a half, and then they took them off, I think, to Manjaca or somewhere like that. And then some buses went, but I don't think they all went. Quite a few of them went on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Utilising that period of time, end of May to the period when you said that they were essentially moved -- during that period of time, sir, did you continue to regularly and continuously work at the iron ore mine in the same capacity as you had prior to the end of May 1992? In essence, did you continue to maintain and operate the water system at the iron ore mine?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you likewise, sir, continue to work in the same shift that you described earlier, namely, 24 hours working, 48 hours off?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in terms of getting a better appreciation for what you did during this time period, maintaining the water pumps at the iron ore mine, did you have to leave the complex where the detainees were in order to perform your duties and obligations in the capacity in which you've described?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I continued doing my work as usual. Because of the nature of those times, I had to move along a certain route. There were pumps that were quite far away, 2 kilometres away. There were surface pumps and deep-level pumps, and then we also had pumps for drinking water. Sometimes there were accidents or pumps broke down or had to fixed, so we would go and fix them. The locksmith then went along with, and we looked after the pumps.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period that the detainees were at the iron ore mine, who was maintaining or providing the security for the iron ore mine?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: The police did, the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any military presence during the time that the detainees were at the iron ore mine in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a military presence, but there was also the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, during that time period when the detainees were in the iron ore mine, was there water provided to them and was there water available to people at the iron ore mine?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, water was available in the Omarska iron ore mine. But when a pump broke down, then we -- water was brought in in tank trucks, and they would use that while the wells were not being used. We also had industrial water, and we had drinking water. We had all types of water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, during the time that the detainees were at the iron ore mine, did they, from time to time, utilise the drinking water that was available at the iron ore mine?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair, sir, to say that the detainees drank the same water that you drank while you were working there on the 24-hour shifts that you've described previously?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, during this shift that you work of 24 on and 48 off, what were your sleeping accommodations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: We slept in the electric workshop, on the work benches that were there. That's where we pump operators and locksmiths and electricians slept usually when we were on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the food, sir, tell us, first, whether or not there was any food provided at the iron ore mine during the period of time that the detainees were there in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Food was delivered. And they had food. But the kitchen was in Omarska, and food was brought from there for the detainees. It was the same kitchen, so the same food was brought in for them and for us. The kitchen was in Omarska, and the food was brought in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair, sir, to say that the detainees ate the same food that you ate while you were working on the 24-hour shift that you previously described?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we had the same food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know a person by the name of Miroslav Kvocka? Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know him. I testified two years ago for Miroslav Kvocka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we understand that, and I believe the Court has been provided with that prior testimony. My question to you, if you can describe for us once again the incident involving Mr. Kvocka, what occurred, and tell us whether you observed it and then describe for us to the best of your recollection what is it that you observed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: I observed that people were brought in in buses. They started getting off and lining up. A soldier ran up. There was commotion. And he started shooting at the people. Kvocka stood in front of them, spread out his arms, and said "Don't shoot. You'll kill the people." I was there. I saw him standing there. And this soldier, I don't know who he was, started shooting. I don't know what happened to the soldier afterwards, but they took him away. And then they took care of things. There were dead and wounded. I could see that. They took the wounded for treatment. Kvocka called in an ambulance. So he sent the wounded people off to hospital. That's what I know about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sir, at other occasions, did you have the unfortunate opportunity to view corpses or dead bodies in or around the iron ore mine in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did see a few corpses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, sir, determine or ask how it was that there were corpses at the iron ore mine in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: I couldn't establish that. I didn't approach them to see better. I wasn't allowed to approach them. It was the military who took care of all that. So I couldn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there restrictions placed upon you as to where you can move within the iron ore mine in the spring and summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. There were restrictions as to where we could move. We couldn't move around. We had to stick to the route that would take us to the place where we had to work. But we couldn't wander around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the water that you provided to the iron ore mine in the spring and summer of 1992, were you ever, sir, ordered or instructed not to provide water for the detainees at the iron ore mine at that time or at any time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Water was delivered regularly. We had to supply water regularly. I've already said that when pumps broke down, drinking water was brought in in tanks, in tank trucks. And we all used that water until the breakdown was fixed. We had a well, but if a pump broke down, we would have to repair it. And then we would have to bring in water. That's what we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, turning to another subject if I may, I couldn't help but notice that you smiled and waved over to us when you arrived in this Trial Chamber. Can you tell us how it is that you know Dr. Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: How could I not know him? He went to school with my son. They are of the same generation. I've known him since childhood, since his childhood. He comes from a good family. I was a little surprised to see that -- to see what had happened. He was young, and he was appointed to this office that he held. And, well, what happened happened. I can't say much, but I know his family, and I knew him as a young man. He was a good boy. He never -- he was never wild. He was never involved in politics. I belong to an older generation, but I could see how people behaved. And all I can say about him was that he was a good man, a good boy, and he was good as a young man. And when he was appointed president of the municipality, we were already practically at war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to try to break down the time period that you knew Dr. Stakic. As you mentioned, you knew him as a child and you knew his family. Can you tell us, sir, at any time during the period that you knew Dr. Stakic as a child growing up, having an ability to appreciate and know his family, was there ever a time period that Dr. Stakic or his family exhibited any ill will, prejudice, or discrimination against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: No. There was no discrimination on their part, nor did he ever do anything like that. We were on good terms with his family. His father and I were on good terms. There were no problems. I don't know what else I can say. As for me, there's nothing more I can say. I can only tell you all the best, and I abide by that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let me go back and just ask you a couple more questions about the Omarska iron ore mine, if I may. With respect to the iron ore mine, was there a period of time when the production ceased, and can you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: The production ceased immediately after the attack on Prijedor. As soon as the attack on Prijedor started, the production ceased because people stopped turning up for work, Muslims and other ethnic groups stopped turning up for work. I didn't see them after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just based on the time line that we have previously established, would that be approximately in late April to late May 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the time range, between April and May. It was not a long period of time, but in any case, that was the period of time when changes were felt. People stopped coming to work. I didn't know why, I just realised that there were no people. And those of us who stayed, continued working. But the production ceased. We stopped exporting the ore, and everything stopped. Only a few of us remained, and we maintained the facilities. That was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Clarify for us, if you may, whether and how it was that there were two systems of water, one for industry and one for drinking, at the iron ore mine, and explain if you will whether you maintained both.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: I maintained both of the systems. I had a few colleagues working with me. We worked in shifts. We had surface pumps, and we had the pumps that were working in the depth. Those were down to 150 metres in the ground. And we also had a big pump, 400 cubic metres of water was being pumped out. I knew the system because that's where I worked. And the pump for the drinking water was a little bit further from there, some 5 or 6 kilometres. From there we had a well from which we transported drinking water to the mine. So those were the two types of water -- pumps. We had a number of pumps. We had the pumps at the mine, and we had the pump for the drinking water which pumped water from the well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, sir, that the industrial water with the high pressure that you've just described, approximately 400 cubic metres of water, that no one is able to drink that water for a number of reasons; one being that the high pressurisation of that water, it would be unable to drink, correct, because the water is coming out quite fast?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: One couldn't drink that water. One could not use it because it was mixed with the sand and particles of iron ore, and it was under high pressure. The diameter of that pump was 20 -- 200 centimetres, and it was under high pressure. We couldn't use it for drinking. We could only use it for maybe washing the cars. It was definitely not the water that could be used for drinking. We had drinking water, wells, that we used to pump out the drinking water, and that is what we used then and it is still being used for the drinking water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rosic. In light of the time, we'll have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We thank you. Prosecution is prepared for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I could start, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rosic, just briefly regarding one of the last --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, could I ask the usher to move the ELMO so we have a line of sight.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll turn towards you so you can see me better and I can see you better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, I appreciate that. Sir, Mr. Ostojic asked you whether it was impossible to drink the high-pressure water because of the pressure. Sir, if you took that water out and put it in a barrel, it's no longer under pressure. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: We never put them in barrels. We conveyed that water into the river, Gomjenica. This was under a very high pressure. The capacity was 400 cubic metres an hour. And there's no way this water could be used for drinking. There were other pumps for sludge that we used because they were under lower pressure and they had a lower capacity. And it couldn't be used for drinking. That water from that big pump could not be used for drinking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not use it for drinking because it would have been unhealthy and inhumane to give that water to someone to drink. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: It wasn't used, not only because it was not humane. It was just not usable. We didn't use it. I told you, we had a well where there was drinking water, and then we would use tankers that -- to bring that water from the well for the purposes of the kitchen and for drinking. The industrial water was not for drinking. It could only be used for industrial purposes and maybe for washing the cars. And in any case, that was -- that was the water under very high pressure, and we didn't use it for drinking. It was not drinkable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it used for washing cars in the vicinity of the garage? Is that where the cars were washed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: We have a pump in a location called Praliste, the washing spot. This is where we used to wash our industrial machines, the dumpers and other machines. There was a pump there, and then you would switch it on. There would be water coming under the pressure. And we used it to wash the machinery and the vehicles, the dumpers, and the bigger-size vehicles and transport means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was at the end of the hangar building. Would that be correct, just past the hangar building, the pump?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Correct. Yes, it was outside the hangar, towards the mining surface.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did the guards that were -- the people that were guarding the detainees, did they have access to that area? Could they wash their cars with that pump?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: They probably did. Actually, yes, they did wash their cars there. I'm sure they used that spot to wash their cars when they had to wash them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Rosic, please tell us, what was -- what do you remember about when the prisoners first arrived? Can you describe the scene, the time of day, and what you recall about the first time you realised that the Omarska mine was going to be used to detainee people.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: I saw people being brought in. That's when I first saw them. Otherwise, there was nothing there before. There were no preparations underway. We didn't know anything. We didn't know that anything like that would happen until the army brought in the people and just put them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were no changes that you noticed before that or no confrontations between the army and the personnel at the mine before the prisoners showed up on the buses. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you mistreated or threatened in any way by the army or police that showed up with the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Well, we were not threatened by them because it was our work obligation to maintain the facilities. We were all, so to say, elderly people. Some of them were invalids, so they were not mobilised. They didn't have any military engagement. We were told where we were to move. We could move to the -- up to the pump, and we were marked, so we were -- they were able to recognise us. We had to behave the way they told us in order to avoid any incidents. And that's how we behaved all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you continue to have the same supervisors? Did you continue to consider yourself employed by the Ljubija mine company after the prisoners arrived?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, for a short period of time after that, and then I was retired. I reached a certain age, so I worked for about a year or two years after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So during the time that the prisoners were there, you and the other personnel from the mine continued to work for the mine maintaining the equipment and providing basics such as water and electricity to that facility. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, we continued working. But the mine did not operate. We maintained the facilities and that was all. There was actually no work going on there, and it is the same situation until this very day. Things are just being maintained, but nothing is happening. There are no developments. The iron ore is not excavated. So the mine is at a standstill. There's just a certain level of maintenance going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So just so I'm absolutely clear, I want to understand that just during that time that the prisoners were there, from the end of May until August of 1992, during all that time, did you continue to be an employee of the Ljubija mine company? Was that your employer?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Our employer was Mirko Babic. He was the closest to us. And the director of the mine was Tomo Vujicic at the time. And that's how things were at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not asking you your supervisors. I appreciate that information. But these two men that you just mentioned were employees also of the Ljubija mine company. Isn't that correct, all of you were employees of the Ljubija mine company?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: That is correct. But our immediate supervisor was Babic. He was in the mine, and he was our supervisor of all of us who were doing the maintenance. He was our immediate supervisor in the mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Now, you said during your direct testimony that the mine stopped operating after the attack on Prijedor. And I just want to be sure I understand what you're talking about. When you say "the attack on Prijedor," which event are you talking about? Well, let me just --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Prijedor was attacked by other ethnic groups, by Muslims, I suppose. Prijedor was attacked, and there was some sort of a misunderstanding, some sort of an accident. I don't know what had preceded all that. I don't know what happened before. That's what I heard. I didn't see anything. I didn't see what happened. So I can't give you the exact answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. It helps what you've said because we know now that that has been established as the 30th of May, that event. Now, prior to that day, there already were prisoners in the camp, correct, a few days before that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: No, there weren't any. Before that, there weren't any. The first ones arrived in several buses. And before that, there were no detainees in the mine. I was there, and I am sure of what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, these buses, when they arrived that first time, did you hear -- let me withdraw that and start again, sir. Did you hear about an incident at the Hambarine, at a checkpoint Hambarine, on the 22nd of May?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was not in the position to know that. I was rather far away. I didn't go there. On the way to my workplace, I didn't have to pass through that place, so I really don't know. I can't tell you anything about that. It's a completely different thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you for your clear answer. And there's no need to explain yourself if you didn't hear about it, that's sufficient. Did you hear about the army's attack on Hambarine on the 23rd of May and the attack on the Kozarac area on the 24th of May?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: I heard. I heard that there was an attack. But I wasn't there. I can't tell you anything about that. I know that this did happen, and the war had already started. Let's be clear on that. It was already a war. The war was going on, and things just started happening that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not asking you to tell us anything you don't know --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so we can establish a time, isn't it correct that the prisoners arrived after this attack on Kozarac, after the army's action in the Kozarac area, the prisoners started arriving at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't. The first detainees arrived in late May, towards the end of May. That is when the first prisoners arrived. I remember that there was nobody there before, and it was my shift when the first buses arrived, and I saw them. Before that, I didn't notice anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said it was on your shift when the first buses arrived. Prior to that, was there any military or police presence in the camp, before the buses showed up?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: No, nothing. From then onwards, the army came, the police, and the guards. Before that time, there was nobody. On that day, I arrived at the mine as every other day before that, and I was taken by surprise. And then I heard that things had happened, some bad things had happened, and that's when I saw the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time of day would your shift begin? You said it was a 24-hour shift. From what hour --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: In the morning. 7.00 in the morning is the time when I had to show up for work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that clear answer. So at 7.00 in the morning, one day you showed up for work, and what time did these buses, the first group of prisoners that you saw, arrive?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: The buses had already reached the gate when I turned up for work. They were already there. But they were still on the buses. The troops accompanied them. They had reached the gate of the mine, so it was very early that morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you talked about -- you testified in the Kvocka case, as you told us, and talked about an incident where Mr. Kvocka had stopped a soldier who was shooting at some men coming off the bus, buses. Was this a different incident, a different group of buses, than the ones that you saw that had first arrived at the camp? Was this a different day?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: That was on the second day. A few buses came, and as the people started getting off the buses, they were lined up. And all of a sudden, all hell broke loose when an unknown soldier ran up to them. Later on, I heard that somebody, a member of his family had been killed. He started shooting at the line of people. He was then stopped. The police removed him from the scene. That's what I saw on the second day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you for that answer. So it was a different day. And do you recall that that day, your son was visiting you in the Omarska facility? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. My son came to see what was happening because I didn't come home. There was no -- nobody to replace me, so my son went -- came to check on me. He came behind the hangar, behind that building. He was worried because I didn't come home on time. He didn't know that I -- that my shift had to be extended because there was nobody to replace me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Koumjian. That there is no possibility of remaining doubts, you mentioned two -- and the witness agreed, that there were two different days. The one day the buses arriving, and then the incident two days later. And then you asked "was it that day your son was arriving?" Was it the first day or two days later?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your son was there the day that Mr. Kvocka stopped the soldiers from shooting. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: That is correct. That is exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: It was on that day. Thank you, sir. So much about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that clear answer. So on that day -- well, just briefly, your son, his name is Milenko. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Milenko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Milenko -- where was he coming from? Did he have a job or was he coming from your home? Was he a member of the police or military?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: He came home because he was a member of the police in Banja Luka. He came home. He didn't find me at home. And that's when he decided to come to my workplace to see where I was. That's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time were you living in - forgive my pronunciation - was it Busnovi, a village in the southeast of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher can just put the document S1 on the ELMO just so that all of Your Honours can see where that is exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Busnovi is there, after Omarska, if you travel southwest, you go through Maricka and then Busnovi according to the map. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: That is correct, but just give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Actually, if you can turn to --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: I can see Omarska, Maricka. I've found Busnovi. Tomasica is also here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if you can just point to the map, not on the screen but on this map on your right, sir. Then we can all see it on the screen. If you point to the map on the right to Busnovi.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Well, this is Busnovi, this is Maricka, and this is Tomasica. You can see it here. It's very easy to find these places on the map. This is -- Tomasica is another village very close to Busnovi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for the help, sir. That's all we need on the map. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I was looking at the screen, and I didn't know I was supposed to look at the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could the usher please move the ELMO back so I can see the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, now you said you were late that day. When your son arrived about, what time of day was it? Was it still the morning? Was it in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Well, must have been sometime in the afternoon, around noon or after the noon. Sometime around that time. I was not looking at my watch, because I didn't know at the time that somebody would ask me to remember the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's perfectly understandable. And did you -- was this the day of the attack on Prijedor that you mentioned when the non-Serbs attacked Prijedor? Was this the same day?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same day. It was that same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you take it, sir, that we've established in this case, through other witnesses and newspaper articles, that that was the 30th of May, would it be correct that your shift had started on the 29th of May, the day before?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I believe that my shift was the first shift which starts at 7.00, and we usually worked for 24 hours. And then we would be off for 48 hours. And yes, it was my shift on that day. It happened on my shift when the buses arrived. I was there. And it was my shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. My confusion was I thought that you had been -- that your son came because you had stayed late on your shift, and that's why your son had arrived that day. So am I mistaken about that? Or was this incident that happened with Mr. Kvocka, was this after your regular shift or during your regular shift?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Maybe I did stay late. I may have extended my shift. And my son came to see what I was doing, what had happened to me, why I hadn't come home. I extended my shift because there was no one to replace me. So I think I must have extended it because when they arrived, I stayed on. I would stay on for two or three shifts when it was necessary at the time. There were times when I had to extend my shift if there was no one to replace me. I couldn't just abandon my workplace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So thank you for trying so hard to recollect these things that happened a long time ago. So if your shift started on the 29th, the previous two days, you would have been off, the 28th and the 27th, and the last day you would have worked before that would have been the 26th of May. Is that correct? Does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the first group of prisoners that you saw would have arrived the 26th of May. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether this date is correct. I can't be sure. Was it the 26th or the 28th? I don't know. I can't tell you the exact date when it was because I didn't know I would need to know this. I didn't know I had to remember these dates. I would have noted them down had I known. But I can't be a hundred per cent sure whether it was the 26th or the 28th. It's hard to tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly that's understandable. But it definitely was not the same day that Mr. Kvocka stopped the soldier from shooting that the first group of prisoners arrived. They had arrived before that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't the same day. That was later. It wasn't on the same day. I remember it was not the same day. It was later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I understand you've just told us several times that you didn't know you had to note it down. It's the first time you've had to remember these dates. I presume, then, that aside from testifying in Mr. Kvocka's case, you never were interviewed or testified in a court about what you saw happen at the Omarska camp. In the Republika Srpska, in Prijedor, Banja Luka, you never were interviewed by the police or were asked to give testimony in a court. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: You mean at home? You mean at home, or you mean here? No, no, no, no one asked me to testify. Only in the Kvocka case here in this Tribunal two years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you mentioned Mr. Kvocka. Is it correct that he was dismissed from the Omarska camp several weeks after this incident?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Or he may have been moved to another place. But he was no longer in Omarska. Kvocka was sent away somewhere else. He was not in Omarska. I never saw him in Omarska any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know or did you hear anything about why it was that Mr. Kvocka was taken out of his position at the camp?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: I heard that he was replaced. Well, he had a wife of a different ethnicity, and he had brought his brothers-in-law to stay with him, and they noticed that. And they exerted pressure on him to bring them to the collection centre, Kvocka. And then they moved him. They gave him a different assignment. That's what I heard. And he had to bring them to the centre. And then he was assigned to another duty. I don't know where, but he wasn't there any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your understanding was that he was taken out of the camp because of assistance he gave to brother-in-laws who were Muslim. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in your work in the Omarska camp, did anyone warn you that there were mines around the camp that you should avoid?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: There were at some distance, around the petrol station. They told us not to go there. There was a petrol station up there, and they put something there. I didn't go there. I didn't have any need to go there. And they said we weren't allowed to move there. But I wasn't interested in that. I didn't go there. I used another route where the entrance to the pit was. It was about a hundred metres down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when it was that those mines were placed at that location?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't know. I didn't see that. I don't know when they were put there. But we were told to move around at night because I went, made the rounds of the pump at night as well, but I was told not to go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Going back to this first group of prisoners that arrived, not the time that Mr. Kvocka stopped the soldier, but the first group of prisoners that arrived at the camp, I believe you said - am I correct - that there were about 20 buses that arrived?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. About 20. I didn't count them. But there were about 20 buses, a long, long convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And realising again that it's only an estimate, can you give us an estimate of about how many people were on each bus, how many prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: I'm sure there were at least about 50, because the buses were full. A bus can usually hold 50 or 60 people. These were large buses. So it may have been that number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were these people dressed, the people that were on the bus that became the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Some were in civilian clothes, and some were in uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the uniforms that you saw.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Their uniforms were greenish. They had a different sort of uniform. It was kind of greenish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you see women in the Omarska camp when you were working there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were women there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the women held in the camp?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: The women were in the administration building. They were held separately. They had their own accommodation there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of these women in uniform when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any. I didn't see any in uniform. But I never visited them up there. I didn't need to go there, nor was I allowed to. But they were there in separate quarters in the administration building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you weren't allowed to, is it correct that you did not have access to all parts of the camp; there were certain restrictions placed on you by the police who were guarding the prisoners. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't allowed to go there. They said, "You don't have to go there," so they prevented me from going, although I had colleagues there. But I wasn't allowed to go and contact them. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, for my next question, I'm going to ask you, if for any reason, you'd rather say this in private session, so it's not public, just let us know. Did you recognise colleagues, friends, neighbours among the prisoners at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO ROSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Colleagues from work. There were colleagues from work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the women that were held prisoner? And again, if you'd like to give this in private session, it's not a problem, if you don't want to name names in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think to be on the safe side, let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This brings me to the core question of tomorrow. Mr. Lukic, may I ask you, based on your contacts you had in the meantime, what is your real time estimate for tomorrow's videolink?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we scheduled this witness for Thursday knowing that that's a short day knowing because he is the shortest witness we have for the videolink. So we hope we will be able o finish Mr. Rosic and the witness for tomorrow, tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this would mean that we start at 2.15 tomorrow with the videolink, and we try immediately afterwards to conclude your testimony. So I would ask you to standby tomorrow, and I have to ask you please refrain from any contacts. Don't speak about your testimony with one of the parties, the Prosecution counsel or Defence counsel. And in case, by chance, you meet any other person you know from the area or related to your own testimony, please don't discuss what is part of your testimony here in this courtroom. I think we can rely on you. So therefore, we will then proceed tomorrow. I have to mention, it shouldn't be forgotten, we have to conclude tomorrow a quarter to 5.00. And in addition it shouldn't be forgotten that there is a 65 ter (i) conference in Room M177 at 10.00 on Friday, 28 February. Any further urgent matters to be resolved immediately? This is apparently not the case. Mr. Rosic, I have to thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. I'm alone here. I have no one to talk to. I'm the only witness here. And I can't hear anything from anyone, nor do I need to hear. I know what I saw. I can tell you that on my own. I abide by everything I said. I don't evade any questions. I know what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I wish you a nice evening here in The Hague. The trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, a quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: at 7.05 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 27th day of February, 2003, at 2.15 p.m. 25
